newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: China state banks should shun bad firms-minister.
newsitem.headline: China state banks should shun bad firms-minister.

text.p: China's state banks are under no obligation to give lines of credit to loss-making state-owned enterprises, which should be left to sink or swim, Chinese finance minister Liu Zhongli said on Saturday.
But Liu, attending an Asia Pacific finance ministers meeting in Cebu, said most of the loss-making firms in China's state industrial sector were those which were relatively small in size.

"It is quite right for the People's Bank of China (the central bank) to use differing credit levels as a means of dealing with enterprises depending on their condition, good or bad," Liu said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.

"The banks will supply credit for those enterprises performing well to fund their continued operation, but the commercial (major state) banks will naturally not provide credit for loss-making enterprises, therefore it is inevitable that they will have to go bankrupt," he said. The loss-making firms could also choose to merge, he said.

A large proportion of China's state-owned enterprises are effectively bankrupt but are still supported by the state banks because the Beijing leadership does not want to risk the social instability that would be caused by mass closures.
Some parts of the country are trying to push through reforms and mergers of poorly-run state firms, but it has to be conducted with care in order to avoid mass unemployment, analysts say.

China announced last month that the four major state banks would from next year be given far greater authority over the placement and size of working capital loans of up to one year's duration, largely to the state firms.
The target for abolishing controls on fixed capital credit has been set for the year 2000.

"The object of our reforms is to make sure the larger state enterprises perform on a profitable basis, while we take a flexible approach to the smaller enterprises," Liu said. "That is, if they are not performing very well, they can be allowed to merge, go bankrupt, or be sold."
